title_original: Cozy escapism or festive trash? How Netflix holiday movies took over Christmas
excerpt_original: The so-bad-it’s-good holiday film has become a new festive tradition. Stars Maddie Ziegler and Dennis Quaid explain why they’re so hard to resist “With the state of the world right now, people want an escape,” says Maddie Ziegler. The 24-year-old performer first shot to fame on…

blocks.text: “W ith the state of the world right now, people want an escape,” says Maddie Ziegler. The 24-year-old performer first shot to fame on the Lifetime reality show Dance Moms in 2011, before becoming the unlikely muse of the publicity-shy singer Sia , which led to a role in Steven Spielberg ’s West Side Story. Ziegler’s latest project is In a Holidaze , a fuzzy Christmas movie that comes to Netflix on 2 December. “I’ve actually never done a romcom before,” she says, speaking on a recent Zoom call from Los Angeles. “I grew up loving Christmas movies so much, so when this came into my lap, I was so excited.’”

In the film, Ziegler plays Maelyn – a restless twentysomething who finds herself trapped in a holiday time-loop, where she’s forced to relive the same Christmas at her family’s picturesque cabin until she learns to trust her gut and take chances on what makes her happy. This sugary-sweet movie might be new territory for Ziegler, but it’s exactly the type of film we’ve come to expect from Netflix. The streamer’s Christmas originals usually revolve around romance and family, with an aesthetic quality and winking irony that feels similar to Hallmark – the American card-maker turned movie giant, whose very name is synonymous with cliches.

While Hallmark is churning out at least 34 new Christmas films this year, Netflix has a more modest slate of six originals. These include A Dog’s Perfect Christmas , starring romcom royalty Dennis Quaid, and Guarding Stars , where Gossip Girl alum Leighton Meester plays a no-nonsense bodyguard who is tasked with protecting a rock star played by Gilmore Girls heartthrob Jared Padalecki. (No prizes for guessing what happens next …) Generally, Netflix’s Christmas films only have a tenuous relationship with reality and – how do I put this? – aren’t exactly aiming for the coveted 100% Rotten Tomatoes score. (They could be kindly described as “light-hearted escapism”, or less so as … “festive trash”.) But regardless, their undeniable popularity suggests that, for Netflix subscribers at least, escaping into a so-bad-it’s-good film has become its own Christmas tradition.

The rise of Netflix’s Christmas content reads like a streaming-era fairytale. It all started in 2017, when A Christmas Prince became a surprise hit. The cookie-cutter Christmas tale, which chronicled an unlikely romance between an aspiring journalist (Rose McIver) and a prince (Ben Lamb), spawned two sequels in 2018 and 2019. Over the next couple of years, Netflix dropped more Christmas movies, including The Princess Switch and the medieval-inspired The Knight Before Christmas, both of which starred High School Musical’s Vanessa Hudgens. By 2020, the streamer amped up its output to seven original Christmas movies – a number that has held relatively steady since then, alongside a massive back-catalogue of Christmas classics. (This year, subscribers can stream Love Actually and The Holiday, alongside some, ahem, slightly lesser-known acquisitions such as A Very English Christmas and Christmas at the Palace .)

blocks.caption: Josh Whitehouse and Vanessa Hudgens in The Knight Before Christmas. Photograph: Brooke Palmer/Netflix

blocks.text: Netflix’s festive movies often feel like they purposefully riff off existing films. Common motifs include unlikely romances, time-travel, body-switching, fictional royalty from non-existent countries, and all kinds of low-stakes situations that, of course, must be fixed in time for Christmas. During a conversation with In a Holidaze writer and director Tiffany Paulsen, I described the film as “ Groundhog Day meets The Family Stone ”. Paulsen was thrilled to be in the company of such “amazing, iconic references”, noting that the core of every Christmas movie comes back to family. “The holiday tradition is people coming together, whether that’s your traditional family or your chosen family,” she says. “That’s the universal element in all of these stories.”

These films also tap into nostalgia. Even the mere mention of 90s heartthrob Quaid makes millennials like me long for the days of watching the 1998 classic The Parent Trap on VHS tape. Quaid, who stars in A Dog’s Perfect Christmas, tells me that new festive films tap into a “yearning” for a time before smartphones. “The 90s was about family,” he says, “and it was the last decade of analogue.” He even jokes about how, in today’s hyper-connected world, the twins in The Parent Trap would have been easily rumbled. “Those kids would have been tracked on their phones by parental controls,” Quaid laughs. “They would have been like, ‘What’s this international bill I’m getting on my account?!’”

blocks.caption: Brooke Lena Johnson and Dennis Quaid in A Dog’s Perfect Christmas. Photograph: Diyah Pera/Netflix

blocks.text: The Parent Trap made Lindsay Lohan a generational star, so it’s no surprise that she has also appeared in a handful of Netflix’s festive films. In fact, it’s become a pattern for these movies to be a vehicle for actors who first made their name in TV shows or films from the 2000s to reconnect with their (now slightly older) audience. This year, Padalecki and Milo Ventimiglia – who fans first met as romantic rivals in Gilmore Girls – both appear in separate Netflix Christmas films. Padalecki tells me that the rise of streaming platforms, plus the ability to watch TV virtually anywhere on any device, has given the show – and by extension, him – a whole new level of cultural relevance. “When I was on Gilmore Girls , in 2000-2005, it wasn’t yet the show it is now,” he says. “It was big, but it wasn’t like everybody has seen it and re-watches it every fall.”

In fact, Padalecki thinks Netflix might have tapped him for this project because the millennial ritual of rewatching the show makes him feel innately familiar to people. “With TV, you’re in their home, you’re playing in the background when they’re cooking dinner, or they’re taking out the garbage, or helping their kids with homework,” he says. “And as they’re doing that, they’re hearing your voice.”

blocks.caption: Zoe Kosovic, Henrik Bosovich, Leighton Meester and Jared Padalecki in Guarding Stars. Photograph: Netflix/PA

blocks.text: For the stars of these movies, it’s not difficult to see why Netflix – the world’s largest streaming service, with over 300 million subscribers in about 190 countries – would be an appealing platform. Ziegler, who has grown up in the era of split screens and endless scroll, tells me that her “goal” was to one day appear in a Netflix project, and that she had zero qualms about joining the often-maligned genre of cutesy festive films. But the deeper question is why Netflix’s Christmas output is so tilted towards making films that feel so similar to Hallmark movies – albeit with slightly more onscreen diversity and star power. The streamer doesn’t seem focused on, for example, making the next great Christmas romcom, such as Bridget Jones’s Diary, or an Oscar-winning film like The Holdovers , which became a melancholic Christmas classic almost instantly.

The answer might be that Netflix’s cheap and cheerful Christmas movies are surprisingly popular. A representative for Netflix UK tells me that, every week in December 2025, there were six or more holiday movies in the UK’s weekly top 10, which rose to seven in 10 in the final two weeks of the year. On the day I spoke to Quaid, A Dog’s Perfect Christmas had just become Netflix’s top movie globally – despite a response from reviewers I will charitably describe as lukewarm . And as Americans prepare to travel home for Thanksgiving, Guarding Stars also hit the global top spot.

blocks.caption: Milo Ventimiglia and Cathryn Michon in A Dog’s Perfect Christmas. Photograph: Diyah Pera/Netflix

blocks.text: Making a higher volume of content that can be consumed quickly is consistent with Netflix’s audience strategy – and it’s an approach that has drawn criticism. Last year, the Guardian reported on Netflix’s move towards algorithm-driven content with mass appeal. Writer Phil Hoad’s story had no shortage of frustrated quotes from the streamer’s creative partners, including a blockbuster director who described its strategy as “the stifler of originality and creativity”. While Netflix has struck gold with critically acclaimed dramas such as Adolescence and The Diplomat, these shows feel increasingly like the exception, which might be because, as Hoad writes, “spread-betting on an inoffensive mainstream, rather than riskily hunting down artistic excellence, is better for sustaining subscriber numbers.”

The conundrum for Netflix is whether its undeniably impressive metrics translate into content that is genuinely loved by audiences. But even so, its Hallmark-coded Christmas films feel like an exception to the rule, because it seems like a sense of disassociation is actually the point. “Holiday movies are sort of like a safety net where everything’s going to be OK,” says Christina Hobbs, one half of Christina Lauren, the duo who co-wrote the 2020 novel that In a Holidaze is based on. “I just think people really need that right now.” Lauren Billings, her co-writer, agrees that these stories often soothe the anxieties of younger viewers in particular. “There’s not enough jobs, young people think they’re never going to make it, or they’re never going to be able to buy a house,” she says. “And so I think that we crave that sense of comfort and reassurance.”

Films like A Dog’s Perfect Christmas might not be winning the Palme d’Or at Cannes any time soon, but considering that there is a long tradition of Christmas-themed art purposefully playing with our ideas of “high” and “low” brow, it’s difficult to take umbrage with films that allow people to briefly escape into a world of cliches and candy canes. “I feel like what we do is so important,” says Paulsen. “We give people a moment of love and warmth and laughter, as cheesy as it sounds.”
In a Holidaze is out on Netflix on 2 December; A Dog’s Perfect Christmas and Guardian Stars are out now
